intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that nanophthalmos-4 (NNO4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM98 gene (615949) on chromosome 17q11.2.

checks.explanation: The abstract places TMEM98 in the 17p12-q12 linked region. The more specific 17q11.2 band is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Nanophthalmos-4 is an autosomal dominant ocular disorder in which affected individuals have small eyes with short axial length, usually with hyperopia that is often high (Awadalla et al., 2014; Khorram et al., 2015). The degree of hyperopia varied between families (Khorram et al., 2015).

checks.claim: Nanophthalmos-4 is an autosomal dominant ocular disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: To perform a clinical and genetic investigation of a large white family with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes the family's nanophthalmos as autosomal dominant.

checks.claim: Individuals affected by nanophthalmos-4 have small eyes with short axial length.
checks.evidence_quote: Nanophthalmos is a congenital disorder characterized by small eyes
checks.explanation: Small eyes are stated directly. Short axial length follows from the diagnostic cutoff (axial length under 20.0 mm) and the mean axial length of 17.6 mm.

checks.claim: Individuals affected by nanophthalmos-4 usually have hyperopia, which is often high.
checks.evidence_quote: with the main complications being severe hyperopia and angle-closure glaucoma.
checks.explanation: Severe hyperopia is named as a main complication, and affected members had a mean refraction of +11.8 D.

checks.explanation: Contrasts with +13.0 D in pedigree 991-F.

paragraphs.text: Yu et al. (2009) reported a 5-generation Chinese family in which 9 members, aged 6 to 66 years, had isolated bilateral microphthalmia from birth. Hyperopia ranged from +4.50 to +11.50 diopters (mean +8.00), and axial length ranged from 18.22 to 20.26 mm (mean 19.29 mm). Three patients older than 50 years had angle-closure glaucoma or occludable angles, with raised intraocular pressure, which progressed despite trabeculectomy. Two of them (III10 and III15) developed atrophia bulbi despite repeated surgeries and had no light perception in the affected eye. Learning disabilities were seen in one-third of cases. All 9 patients had a normal karyotype. On histology, the sclera showed diffusely swollen, twisted or frayed collagen fibers mixed with normal fibers; in the atrophied globes, collagen alignment was disrupted, the sclera was about 3 times normal thickness, and pigment cell proliferation and bone-like tissue were seen.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) reported 2 pedigrees with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos, both showing high penetrance over at least 4 generations. In pedigree 991-F, a Caucasian family of German heritage from the United States, 6 of 10 examined members were diagnosed with nanophthalmos and 3 more were affected according to the family history. Where measured, axial lengths ranged from 16.7 to 17.4 mm, and refractions ranged from +11.125 to +14.125 D. Mean axial length was 17.1 mm and hyperopia was about +13 D.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the large white South Australian family NNO-SA1 with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos, Awadalla et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene, resulting in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. Exome sequencing found this to be the only novel missense variant in the linkage region that segregated with the disease. It was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls. By RT-PCR, TMEM98 was expressed in all ocular tissues tested, including sclera and optic nerve head. The authors concluded that TMEM98 was most likely the cause of disease in this family, and described it as the first gene identified for autosomal dominant nanophthalmos.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) studied 2 pedigrees with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. In pedigree 991-F, from the United States, they performed exome sequencing in an affected member (IV-3) and identified a his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene. Of the 4 candidate variants, only H196P was coinherited with nanophthalmos, was absent from healthy family members, and had pathogenic scores on all 3 sequence analysis systems. Sanger sequencing showed that all other affected members of the pedigree carried the mutation.

paragraphs.text: In the second pedigree studied by Khorram et al. (2015), 951-N from the Mariana Islands, Sanger sequencing identified a novel 34-bp heterozygous deletion in the TMEM98 gene (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg). The deletion spanned the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4. It was found in all 11 affected members tested and was absent from 4 healthy family members. It was predicted to eliminate a splice site and cause premature termination. Both TMEM98 mutations found by Khorram et al. (2015) were absent from public databases and affected conserved sequences.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the large white South Australian family NNO-SA1 with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos, Awadalla et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.577G-C transversion in exon 8 of the TMEM98 gene, resulting in an ala193-to-pro (A193P) substitution. The variant was found by exome sequencing. It was the only novel missense variant in the linkage region on chromosome 17 that segregated with the disease. It was absent from the Exome Variant Server database and from 285 local white controls. Sixteen of 35 available family members had nanophthalmos, with a mean refraction of +11.8 D and a mean axial length of 17.6 mm.

paragraphs.text: Khorram et al. (2015) identified a his196-to-pro (H196P) mutation in the TMEM98 gene by exome sequencing in pedigree 991-F, a Caucasian family of German heritage from the United States with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos. Affected members had high hyperopia (about +13 D) and a mean axial length of 17.1 mm. The mutation was coinherited with nanophthalmos, was absent from healthy family members and from public databases, and had pathogenic scores on 3 sequence analysis systems. Sanger sequencing showed that all affected members of the pedigree carried it.

paragraphs.text: In pedigree 951-N, a Micronesian Pacific Islander family from the Mariana Islands with autosomal dominant nanophthalmos, Khorram et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous 34-bp deletion in the TMEM98 gene (c.694_721delAGAATGAAGACTGGATCGAAGATGCCTCgtaagg). The deletion spanned the last 28 bp of exon 4 and the first 6 bp of intron 4. It was detected in all 11 affected members tested, was absent from 4 healthy family members and from public databases, and was predicted to eliminate a splice site and cause premature termination. Affected members had a mean axial length of 17.4 mm and milder hyperopia (mean +3.93 D) than the US pedigree.
